case_study_insert.main_stem: Tarnbrook Kinetic Bearings (TKB) is a partnership in the precision engineering sector, manufacturing ball bearings for electric motors and supplying three motor makers, with a workforce of 72 across two shifts. Founded in 1996 by Kirsten Tarnbrook, it operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. TKB plans to invest $840,000 in a precision-grinding cell for ceramic bearings, financed by a $480,000 bank loan and $360,000 of additional partner capital. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $13.00 a unit and a selling price of $24.00, and produces 45,000 units a year. TKB has a 4.9% defect rate and machine breakdowns that have left 9 customer orders late.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Precision Operations Log — March 2025: 11,250 bearings were tested; the defect rate was 4.9%, down from 6.6%. There were 36 customer returns and 96% passed first inspection. Mean lead time is 16 days, and rework cost $9,400 last quarter. A survey of 320 motor manufacturers found 74% rank precision as the main buying criterion and 61% would pay $0.60 more for ceramic bearings with longer life.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tarnbrook Kinetic Bearings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base rate from 3.50% to 4.25%, affecting all variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage rose 5.4% to $13.30 per hour. (3) Alloy steel and ceramic input costs increased 9.4% year-on-year, while precision-engineering export orders rose 3.1% and energy prices rose 4.8%.

questions.question_text: TKB plans to finance its grinding cell with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for TKB of using additional partner capital instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $360,000 partner capital requires no interest or fixed repayments, so cash flow is protected while TKB services the $480,000 loan and carries fixed costs of $330,000 a year. Funds can instead be used to fix the 4.9% defect rate and the 9 late orders, protecting the $11.00 contribution on 45,000 bearings.

Point 2: Partner capital strengthens commitment from Kirsten Tarnbrook and the other partners, aligning ownership with the $840,000 investment and avoiding the collateral that a bank would require. Unlike a loan, it does not create a creditor who could act if the 16-day lead time slips, though profits must be shared.

For a partnership of 72 workers, partner capital also avoids the 4.25% rate risk on $360,000 and aligns funding with the long term. The $480,000 loan still must be repaid, but the $11.00 contribution on 45,000 units and the 15,000-unit margin of safety are better protected when profits are shared instead of interest being due.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: TKB is launching longer-life ceramic bearings. Consider engineering journals, a motor-industry exhibition, or direct technical presentations to its three motor makers. Which should TKB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Engineering journals: They reach the 74% of surveyed motor makers who rank precision first at low cost, but printed data cannot prove the fall in defect rate from 6.6% to 4.9% and are easily overlooked.

Motor-industry exhibition: A stand allows TKB to show ceramic bearings and discuss the $0.60 premium that 61% would pay, building trust. Costs are high for a partnership funding an $840,000 cell, and most visitors are not the three buyers who matter.

Direct technical presentations: Engineers can present test data on 11,250 bearings and the 96% first-pass rate directly to the three motor makers, answering precision questions and securing specifications. This is cheap and targeted, though it depends on maintaining good relationships with a few large customers.

With a 15,000-unit margin of safety and $11.00 contribution, TKB needs qualified leads, not mass awareness. Presentations to the three motor makers can demonstrate the 96% first-pass rate on 11,250 bearings and justify the $0.60 premium directly; the 320 surveyed buyers show wider demand, but only three accounts currently matter. A show would waste cash needed for the $480,000 loan, and journals alone cannot prove the precision that wins specifications.

Test data from the 11,250 bearings should be central to each presentation, because 74% rank precision first.

Recommendation: TKB should choose direct technical presentations, supported by journal adverts. They target the exact buyers and demonstrate the precision that underpins the $0.60 premium. The exhibition is rejected as costly and untargeted; journals alone are rejected because they cannot prove the quality needed to win specifications.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two promotional options applied to TKB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three options in context with a justified recommendation rejecting the exhibition and journals alone.

questions.question_text: TKB has a 4.9% defect rate and flat, democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for TKB of consulting its workforce of 72 through quality circles.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles let the 72 workers investigate the 4.9% defect rate and machine breakdowns using their own operating knowledge, so fixes come from the people closest to the grinders. Democratic leadership makes this consultation genuine, raising commitment and reducing the $9,400 rework bill while protecting the $840,000 investment.

Point 2: Involvement satisfies esteem needs under Maslow and encourages shared responsibility for the 36 returns and 16-day lead time. With flat structures, ideas reach Kirsten Tarnbrook quickly, so output of 45,000 units can recover after breakdowns and the 61% willing to pay $0.60 more are not lost.

At 45,000 units divided by 72 workers, or 625 units per worker, consultation can lift output without new fixed cost. Quality circles fit the flat democratic structure and give the 74% of buyers who rank precision first evidence that the 4.9% defect rate is being addressed, protecting the $0.60 premium.

Consultation therefore supports both motivation and the 625-unit-per-worker target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: TKB needs to address its 4.9% defect rate. Consider internal promotion or external recruitment of skilled grinders. Which should TKB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal promotion: Promoting existing workers rewards loyalty, suits the flat democratic structure and keeps the 72-strong team stable. Promoted operators know the processes behind the 96% first-pass rate, so the 4.9% defect rate is less likely to rise during the $840,000 grinding-cell installation. The risk is that the partnership lacks the precision-grinding skills needed.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced grinders brings the expertise the cell requires and can help cut the 36 returns, but recruitment costs and induction take time, and outsiders may clash with the partnership culture, threatening the 16-day lead time.

Progress should be measured on the 4.9% defect rate, the 36 returns and the 11,250 bearings tested, with monthly checks while the $840,000 cell is installed. The insert gives no salaries or course fees, so none are fabricated; the decision rests on keeping knowledge inside a 72-worker partnership and protecting the 625-unit-per-worker productivity. External recruits would need induction on the grinding cell, risking the 16-day lead time when nine orders are already late and the 30,000-unit break-even must be met. Targeted hiring only for absent skills limits that disruption, and internal promotion signals a career path that retains the precision skills the partnership depends on.

Stable staffing protects the $20.33 unit-cost benchmark.

Decision: TKB should choose internal promotion with targeted external hiring only for the specific grinding skills absent internally. Promotion protects morale and keeps knowledge in the 72-worker team; broad external recruitment is rejected because it is costlier and could disrupt the culture and the 9 late orders.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of internal and external recruitment applied to TKB's skills and defect problem.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both recruitment routes with a justified decision rejecting wholesale external hiring.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TKB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $330,000 ÷ ($24.00 − $13.00) = $330,000 ÷ $11.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $24.00 − $13.00 = $11.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $11.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TKB's management can use this cost, break-even and productivity data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the break-even output of 30,000 units with actual production of 45,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 15,000 units, so they know how far demand can fall before TKB makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $11.00 shows what each unit adds towards fixed costs of $330,000; for illustration, a $1.00 price cut would reduce contribution to $10.00 and raise break-even to 33,000 units, letting managers test pricing before committing.
3. Average total cost of $20.33 a unit ($330,000 ÷ 45,000 units plus $13.00 variable cost) provides a benchmark each quarter to track the 4.9% defect rate and machine breakdowns and decide whether rework is pushing unit cost above plan.
4. Labour productivity of 625.00 units per worker (45,000 units ÷ workforce of 72) shows whether the $840,000 investment can be handled by the existing team, or whether recruitment is needed before the wage bill rises.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $11.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 45,000 units; illustrative pricing and the $330,000 fixed costs; the $840,000 investment decision; and unit-cost and productivity benchmarking to tackle the 4.9% defect rate and machine breakdowns.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TKB's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TKB's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios is the stronger evidence? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.41 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.67 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.69 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.96 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $100,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $275,000; 2025 current assets = $128,000 + $118,000 + $54,000 = $300,000. For 2024, $275,000 ÷ $195,000 = 1.41, and ($275,000 − $140,000) ÷ $195,000 = 0.69. For 2025, $300,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.67, and ($300,000 − $128,000) ÷ $180,000 = 0.96. All source figures are the $'000 values in Appendix 2.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures, so TKB's short-term financial position has improved. Cash rose from $35,000 to $54,000 and current liabilities fell from $195,000 to $180,000, helping TKB service the $480,000 loan, but receivables grew from $100,000 to $118,000, so cash is tied up with the three motor makers.
The acid test ratio is the stronger evidence of real improvement because it rose from 0.69 to 0.96 without relying on inventories, which are the least liquid current asset.

The insert gives no sector average, so 1.67 and 0.96 cannot be compared with peers and both are single-date figures. The $118,000 receivables from only three customers are a concentration risk: one late payer could undo the 2025 gain before the $840,000 cell is paid for.

Conclusion: TKB's financial position has improved: both liquidity measures are higher in 2025 and the gain survives the exclusion of inventories. Kirsten Tarnbrook should tighten collection from the three customers before more of the $840,000 plan is committed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with some contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities, an explicit answer on the stronger ratio, and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TKB of producing ceramic bearings rather than standard steel bearings.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Ceramic bearings can meet the precision demand of the 74% of surveyed buyers and support the $0.60 premium that 61% would pay, protecting the $11.00 contribution on 45,000 units even with fixed costs of $330,000. They also fit the $840,000 grinding-cell investment.

Disadvantage: Ceramic inputs may cost more, and the insert does not decompose the $13.00 variable cost, so the effect of the 9.4% input-cost rise cannot be quantified precisely. With a 4.9% defect rate and 36 returns, any material inconsistency could delay the 16-day lead time further.

Ceramic bearings must hold the 30,000-unit break-even with $330,000 fixed costs: if the 4.9% defect rate persists, the 36 returns and 16-day lead time will deter the 61% willing to pay $0.60 more. The insert gives no ceramic price, so no cost comparison is invented; the benefit rests on precision demand. The $840,000 cell succeeds only if quality improves.

The 15,000-unit margin of safety makes quality the deciding factor.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 5.4% minimum wage increase to $13.30 and the 9.4% rise in alloy steel and ceramic input costs will affect TKB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
TKB faces three external changes reported in Appendix 3.

Base interest rate 3.50% to 4.25%: If the $480,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $480,000 bank loan = $3,600 a year (0.0075 × 480,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $330,000 and the $840,000 investment, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it completely, though future borrowing would cost more and customers may cut spending.

Minimum wage up 5.4% to $13.30: With a workforce of 72, this raises the wage bill on every production hour and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay rates, so no defensible annual total can be invented; against the given productivity of 625.00 units per worker, the rise is absorbable only if output per worker holds, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $11.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

9.4% alloy steel and ceramic input costs: The insert does not decompose the $13.00 variable cost per unit, so only a labelled upper-bound illustration is honest: if the entire $13.00 were exposed, the rise would add 0.094 × $13.00 = $1.222 a unit, or $54,990 a year at 45,000 units. This upper-bound figure is much larger than the $3,600 interest effect and is the key threat to the $840,000 plan.

Conclusion: the 9.4% rise in alloy steel and ceramic input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 45,000 units, directly erodes the $11.00 contribution that justifies the $840,000 plan, and dwarfs the $3,600 interest effect; the wage rise is material but cannot be quantified from the insert. Kirsten Tarnbrook should secure ceramic supply contracts and market the $0.60 longer-life premium.
